newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba moves to counter U.S. Helms-Burton law.
newsitem.headline: Cuba moves to counter U.S. Helms-Burton law.

text.p: Cuba, the target of a U.S. law that seeks to curb foreign investment on the communist-ruled island, unveiled Sunday tough legislation to counter the U.S. threat and to protect existing and future investors.
The draft legislation was approved Sunday by three permanent commissions of Cuba's National Assembly, which will ratify the new law when it meets in full session next Tuesday.

Article One of the proposed legislation declares "null and void" any claim made under the U.S. Helms-Burton law, which threatens penalties against foreign investors in Cuba judged to be "trafficking" in expropriated, formerly U.S.-owned assets.
National Assembly President Ricardo Alarcon, presenting the Cuban draft law, said its aim was to make the U.S. Helms-Burton law "illegal, impossible to apply and without any legal value".

The Cuban legislative response to the Helms-Burton law, introduced by Washington in March, follows similar steps by Canada and Mexico, which are strong opponents of Washington's moves to tighten the U.S economic embargo on Cuba.
So far, executives of a Canadian and a Mexican company have been barred entry from the United States under the Helms-Burton law.

The new Cuban legislation authorises the Cuban government to take all necessary measures to protect existing and future foreign investors on the island. It also declares illegal any kind of assistance given to the U.S. government in its attempts to enforce the Helms-Burton law.

The document re-states the Cuban government's willingness to negotiate fair compensation for U.S. citizens whose holdings in Cuba were nationalised after the 1959 Cuban Revolution, as long as such claims are not pressed under the Helms-Burton law.

Cuba's position is that such compensation discussions should form part of a wider negotiation "on the basis of mutual respect and equality" between Cuba and the U.S., whose relations have been hostile for more than 35 years.
But the Cuban law also declares the right of Cuba's government and citizens to claim compensation for damages caused by U.S. policies and actions against the island.

This includes institutions and citizens affected by the longstanding U.S. economic embargo and victims of acts of sabotage or violence for which the U.S. government could be deemed responsible, before and after the 1959 Cuban Revolution.
Such Cuban claims for compensation could be made to special commissions which would be created by Cuba's Justice Ministry.
Cuban leaders have estimated damage and losses caused to the economy by the U.S. embargo at more than $40 billion.

Cubans would also be able to claim for damage and losses "caused by thieves, swindlers, corrupt politicians, mafiosi, torturers and killers of the Batista tyranny, for whose actions the U.S. government has made itself responsible by promulgating the Helms-Burton law," the Cuban draft legislation said.

The Helms-Burton law permits claims by former Cuban property owners and landowners, whose assets were nationalised after the 1959 Revolution that toppled former dictator Fulgencio Batista, and who later went into exile in the United States and became U.S. citizens.
The Cuban legislation mandates the Cuban authorities to cooperate with other national parliaments and governments in actions to counter the effects of the Helms-Burton law.
One of the formulas suggested to protect foreign investments in Cuba was the transfer of investment interests to trust and investment funds or to other financial bodies.

The draft legislation appeared to be especially tough against those deemed to be helping the U.S. government in its enforcement of the Helms-Burton law. It declared illegal cooperation of any kind with the U.S. authorities, including the supply to "radio and TV stations and other U.S. government propaganda media" of any kind information related to the Helms- Burton law.
